after.abstract: Background: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) and dermatomyositis (DM) are autoimmune diseases that have been proposed as models of cancer immunoediting. Autoantibody-defined subsets show divergent cancer risks, yet malignancy often remains clinically occult. We tested whether circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) can reveal subclinical cancer in new-onset SSc and DM. Methods: We prospectively recruited adults with recent SSc or DM onset. Plasma ctDNA was assessed using a targeted next-generation sequencing panel covering commonly mutated cancer genes. Patients were followed for 18-24 months on average. ctDNA positivity was correlated with subsequent cancer diagnoses. Findings: Among 134 patients (69 SSc, 65 DM), cancer was diagnosed in six (4.5%; three SSc, three DM). ctDNA was detected in four of these six patients (67%) a median of 13 months (range 1.4-17) before clinical diagnosis; in three of four patients, mutations detected in plasma matched those subsequently identified in the same patients primary tumors. ctDNA was also detected in 16 of 128 patients without a cancer diagnosis. ctDNA positivity conferred an 11.4-fold higher risk of malignancy relative to ctDNA negativity and yielded a negative predictive value of 98% and a positive predictive value of 20% for cancer within the observation window. Interpretation: ctDNA testing identified most cancers that emerged within 18 months in new-onset SSc and DM and stratified near-term cancer risk. These findings support larger, interventional trials to determine whether ctDNA-guided surveillance improves timeliness of cancer detection, optimizes imaging and biopsy strategies, and enhances outcomes in patients with SSc and DM.

after.authors: Russell, M. D.; MacKenna, B.; Goodliffe, S.; Roddy, E.; Abhishek, A.; Rowark, S.; Bechman, K.; Gibson, M.; Brown, J.; Cipolletta, E.; Schaffer, A.; Bacon, S.; Mehrkar, A.; de Lusignan, S.; Coates, L. C.; Cope, A. P.; Norton, S.; Goldacre, B.; Galloway, J. B.
after.abstract: Objectives: To evaluate gout management in England before and after publication of a national clinical guideline by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and assess the feasibility of using routinely collected health data to monitor guideline implementation at scale. Design: Observational cohort study with interrupted time-series analysis. Setting: Primary care and hospital admission data, with the approval of NHS England. Participants: 22,618,945 individuals aged 18 to 110 years registered with general practices in England contributing data to the NHS OpenSAFELY Data Analytics Service between July 1, 2016, and June 30, 2025. Intervention: Publication of NICE guidance for the diagnosis and management of gout in June 2022. Main outcome measures: Trends in evidence-based measures for gout management, including new prescription of urate-lowering therapy (ULT) and attainment of a target serum urate below 360 micromol/L. Changes in temporal trends after guideline publication were estimated using interrupted time-series models. Results: Of 245,445 individuals newly diagnosed with gout who had available follow-up, 87,885 (35.8%) were prescribed ULT within 12 months of diagnosis. ULT initiation increased from 26.6% in July 2016 to 43.0% in June 2025; however, the rate of increase slowed after publication of the NICE guideline (change in trend: 0.76 percentage-point decrease per year; 95% CI 0.35 to 1.17; p<0.001). Among 108,380 people initiating ULT at any point after diagnosis, 35,865 (33.1%) had at least one recorded serum urate level below target within 12 months of initiation. Urate target attainment improved modestly following publication of the NICE guideline (change in trend: 1.25 percentage-point increase per year; 95% CI 0.64 to 1.86; p<0.001), although sensitivity analyses suggested that was a continuation of an existing trend rather than a guideline-specific effect. Younger adults and males were more likely to be prescribed ULT but less likely to achieve urate targets than older adults and females. Conclusions: Substantial gaps remain between observed gout management and NICE guideline recommendations, particularly for ULT initiation and serum urate target attainment. Guideline publication was not associated with marked improvements beyond existing temporal trends, highlighting the need for implementation strategies to improve gout care. Importantly, routinely collected health data can be used to monitor guideline implementation at scale and identify priorities for improvement.

after.authors: Cassinat, J. J.; Callan, C.; Liggett, C.; Wright, V.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University of Colorado School of Medicine
after.abstract: Objective: To describe how people use the unapproved peptides BPC-157 and TB-500 for tendon, ligament and muscle injury and what side effects they report. Methods: Using a large language model validated against physician review, we analyzed 92,254 posts and comments from 28,652 users in Reddit's peptide communities from 2021 to 2026. We compared side effects with those reported by users of four other peptides in the same communities. Results: In all, 5,588 users described using BPC-157 and/or TB-500 for a specific musculoskeletal injury, most often a chronic tendon problem of the shoulder, knee or elbow. Only 3.8% of users described physician involvement, and 90.9% of those naming a source bought from research-chemical vendors. The median BPC-157 dose (366 mcg per injection) was about 2.7 times the human-equivalent dose of the 10 mcg/kg rat regimen, and among new users it rose from 300 mcg in 2024 to 500 mcg in 2025. Of those stating an outcome, 79.3% reported improvement, and 36.6% of all users were also in physical therapy. Overall, 27.2% described at least one side effect, most often fatigue, anxiety, anhedonia and insomnia. Anhedonia was more common than among users of the four other peptides (10.2% versus 1.3% of those with side effects). Conclusion: Use of these unapproved peptides for musculoskeletal injury is largely unsupervised, relying on grey-market products at self-selected, rising doses without established safety or efficacy.

after.abstract: Background. As kidneys age, their cells change in arrangement and gene expression. Whether these changes are also present in diabetic kidney disease (DKD), and whether they relate to how quickly kidney function is lost, is not known. Methods. Zero-time biopsies from 24 healthy living kidney donors (aged 36-66 years) and biopsies from 28 patients with DKD were profiled by single-cell-level spatial transcriptomics with a 5,101-gene panel. In the donors, we identified how cell neighborhoods and cell-type gene expression change with age and summarized the expression changes as tissue-aging scores. The scores were applied unchanged to DKD and related to the rate of eGFR decline after biopsy in 24 patients, with adjustment for age, sex, baseline eGFR, and proteinuria. We also estimated the scores from routine periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) slides, using models that did not include the patient being scored. Results. In older donors, immune cells were less often found next to tubular epithelium, and contacts between endothelial cells and podocytes and between stromal and epithelial cells were fewer, although cell proportions changed little. Expression of stress-response and cell-cycle regulators (FOXO3, CDKN1A, BBC3, PINK1, IRAK1, SOCS1) increased. Changes in cell contacts in DKD tissue largely followed the same direction as those in older donors. In DKD, higher tissue-aging scores were associated with faster eGFR loss independently of age, sex, baseline eGFR, and proteinuria (overall score, partial {rho} = -0.61); this held for tubular, endothelial, immune, and parietal epithelial cell scores but not for the podocyte score. Scores estimated from PAS slides correlated with the transcriptomic scores (mean {rho} = 0.62) and were also associated with faster eGFR loss (partial {rho}, -0.44 to -0.56). Conclusions. Healthy kidney aging involves a selective loss of cell contacts together with a coordinated stress-response program. DKD kidneys that carry this aging phenotype lose function faster, and the phenotype can be estimated in part from the routine diagnostic PAS slide.

after.abstract: Neurosurgery is an effective treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), but its success depends on the accurate delineation of the epileptogenic focus, approximated noninvasively by electric and magnetic source imaging (ESI/MSI) of high-density electroencephalography (HD-EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). These modalities have distinct sensitivity profiles; consequently, epileptiform activity detected by one modality may remain undetected by the other. However, the implications of these differences for spike detectability and localization accuracy, and the added value of combined electromagnetic source imaging (EMSI), remain insufficiently characterized under clinically realistic conditions. Here, we characterize HD-EEG and MEG sensitivity profiles and compare ESI, MSI, and EMSI, using realistic simulations with known ground truth. We generated HD-EEG and MEG datasets from cortical, insular, and hippocampal sources across multiple orientations, activated using patient-derived intracranial EEG spike waveforms. Spike sensitivity and localization accuracy were evaluated using dipole scanning, dynamic statistical parametric mapping (dSPM), and linearly constrained minimum variance (LCMV). EEG demonstrated higher spike detection rates and sensitivity for radially cortical sources at gyral crowns and sulcal bottoms (p<0.001), while MEG detected more spikes from tangential cortical sources along sulcal walls (p<0.001). MSI localized tangential sources more accurately than ESI across all methods (p<0.001), while dipole scanning outperformed dSPM and LCMV for cortical and insular sources (p<0.001). EMSI outperformed ESI (p<0.001) but did not improve localization over MSI. These findings suggest that complementary anatomical sensitivities of HD-EEG and MEG may improve epileptogenic source characterization, supporting simultaneous acquisition during the presurgical evaluation of patients with DRE.

after.authors: Lim, C. K.; Brocardo, M.; Hunter, J.; Heads, J. A.; Rowe, D. B.; Furlong, S.; Atkin, J. D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: MND Research Centre, Faculty of Medicine, Health and Human Sciences, Macquarie University
after.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibit heterogeneous functional decline, potentially influenced by systemic metabolic reserve. We investigate whether circulating insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is associated with subsequent functional change in ALS. Serum IGF-1 was measured in 37 participants with ALS and 25 healthy controls. Baseline levels were compared between groups, and across disease-duration defined progression categories. Lagged regression assessed whether prior visit IGF-1 level predicted change in Revised ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R) on the next visit, adjusting for inter-visit interval, body mass index, age and sex. Mixed-effects and sensitivity analyses assessed robustness. Baseline IGF-1 did not differ significantly between controls and ALS (mean + SD: 107.3 + 54.3 vs 132.2 + 68.3 ng/mL, p = 0.12), or across progression categories (F(2, 34) = 0.13, p = 0.88). Across 48 intervals from 23 ALS participants, each 1-SD higher IGF-1 from prior visit was associated with 1.40-point less subsequent {Delta}ALSFRS-R decline (95% CI: 0.03 to 2.77, p = 0.045). Generalised estimating equations yielded a similar association ({beta} = 1.50, p = 0.030), whereas small-cluster robust inference showed wider uncertainty (p = 0.084). Repeated IGF-1 showed an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.69, and the lagged association remained positive in all 23 leave-one-participant-out analyses. The IGF-1-by-time interaction was not significant in a random-slope mixed model (p =0.254). Higher circulating IGF-1 may reflect systemic trophic-metabolic reserve associated with short-term functional preservation in ALS, but limited precision precludes definitive prognostic or causal conclusions.

after.title: Preprint: Optimized phase-targeted auditory stimulation reduces nocturnal spikes in childhood epilepsies
after.authors: Schmidt, E. C.; Wapp, N.-A.; Alessandri, B.; Eberhard, R.; Lederberger, D.; Moser, K.; Imbach, L.; Boelsterli-Heinzle, B.; Ramantani, G.; Fattinger, S.; Huber, R.
after.abstract: Interictal epileptiform discharges, so called spikes, are often strongly activated during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep in childhood epilepsies. In children with pronounced spike activation during NREM - sleep, spike burden can be associated with lifelong impaired cognitive functions. This spike activation is also related to alterations in sleep oscillations, specifically slow waves and spindles, which play essential roles in brain maintenance and maturation. These observations suggest that spikes may disrupt sleep-dependent brain processes that are critical for the development of cognitive functions. Phase-targeted auditory stimulation during NREM sleep delivers brief, non-arousing tones at specific phases of ongoing slow waves to modulate sleep oscillations. Recently, our group showed that isolated, less frequent, and thus less expected, tones engage widespread thalamocortical networks, whereas repetitive, regular trains of tones promote habituation and engage more local corticocortical networks. In this study, we use these contrasting stimulation patterns for a targeted modulation of sleep oscillations and examine their interaction with epileptic spikes. In an initial exploratory study (N = 10; age range: 7.3 - 16.2 years), we used a within-night block design to directly compare responses to the different stimulation patterns. Isolated tones delivered at long interstimulus intervals induced a transient increase in spike rate, whereas down-phase stimulation delivered in trains at short, regular intervals was associated with a significant reduction. We subsequently optimized the train-based paradigm and evaluated stimulation delivered throughout the night in a proof-of-concept study using a counterbalanced, between-night design (N = 5; age range: 4.4 - 10.7 years). Spike density decreased locally in all patients, providing convergent evidence for the effects observed in the exploratory study. With this mechanistically guided approach, we demonstrate that repetitive down-phase auditory stimulation of slow waves results in a local reduction of epileptic spikes. This framework may provide a rational basis for targeted interventions aimed at reducing spikes and related cognitive impairments.

after.title: Preprint: Food-Group Intakes and Depression in Tangerang, Indonesia: An Exploratory Case-Control Study
after.authors: Cipta, D. A.; Saputra, A.; Suryadinata, N.; Siregar, R. U. P.; Rivami, D. S.
after.abstract: Background: Diet may be associated with depression, but evidence on locally consumed food groups in Indonesia is limited. Objectives: To compare food-group intake between people with and without a formal diagnosis of depression in Tangerang, Indonesia, and to explore whether BMI modifies any association. Methods: In this case-control study, cases were psychiatric outpatients with a formal diagnosis of depression. Controls had no formal diagnosis and were recruited through university and community networks. Daily intake of ten food groups was estimated with a semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaire. Intakes were compared with independent-samples t-tests (Welch's test when variances were unequal), overall and stratified by BMI group. Logistic regression estimated the odds of depression per 100 g/day of sweetened beverage intake, adjusted for BMI group, sex, and age, with a sweetened beverage and BMI group interaction term. Results: There were 257 participants: 104 cases and 153 controls. Sweetened beverages were the only food group whose intake differed significantly between groups (approximately 214 vs. 153 g/day; mean difference 61 g/day; 95% CI 18-103; p=0.005). Each additional 100 g/day was associated with higher odds of depression after adjustment (OR 1.29; 95% CI 1.09-1.52). The association appeared stronger in underweight/normal-weight participants (ratio of ORs for overweight/obese vs. underweight/normal 0.70; 95% CI 0.49-0.99; p for interaction=0.046). Conclusions: Higher sweetened beverage intake was associated with depression in this sample, and there was modest evidence that the association differed by BMI group. Because the study is cross-sectional in timing, the case-control samples were selected differently, and many comparisons were made, these findings are exploratory. They do not establish causality.

after.title: Preprint: Communication without dialogue? Framing patient-professional interaction in UK institutional discourse on pregnancy loss
after.authors: Nuttall, L.; Malory, B.
after.abstract: Communication failures are repeatedly implicated in harmful experiences and outcomes in pregnancy care, especially in contexts of loss, yet little is known about how communication itself is represented in the institutional texts that shape expectations of care. This study examines the extent to which communication is discussed, and how patient-healthcare professional interaction is framed, in publicly accessible UK discourse about pregnancy loss. Two corpora comprising texts from seven medical organisations (120,383 words) and eight charities (224,481 words) were divided into healthcare professional-facing and patient-facing sub-corpora. Frequency, semantic keyness, keyword and concordance analyses were conducted using Wmatrix7. In medical discourse, language and communicative interaction were underrepresented, while speech acts associated with unidirectional professional activities such as advising, recommending and referring were overrepresented. Compared with charity texts, medical outputs foregrounded clinical evidence, policy, risk and professional knowledge. Characteristic forms including 'confirmed', 'advised', 'recommended' and 'offered' frequently occurred in passive or agentless constructions that positioned patients principally as recipients of information; patient agency was most visible in 'reporting' symptoms or concerns. Charity discourse more often foregrounded talking, listening, feelings, preferences, wording, lived experience, and patient knowledge; representing communication as active and bidirectional. We argue that UK medical discourse constructs communication primarily as the transmission of authorised knowledge rather than as relational clinical practice, reinforcing a paternalistic distribution of communicative agency. Medical institutions should embed listening, reciprocal dialogue, sensitivity to language preferences, and checks on understanding as core standards of safe pregnancy care.

after.title: Preprint: Hidden overweight and adverse birth outcomes among Asian mothers in the United States, 2016-2023: a population-based repeated cross-sectional study
after.authors: Tasnim Jahan, J.; Afrose, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics, University at Albany, State University of New York, Albany, New York, USA
after.abstract: Background: Standard body mass index (BMI) categories may understate risk in Asian individuals. Lower Asian action points exist, but their relevance to birth outcomes is unclear. Objectives: To estimate the proportion of normal-weight Asian mothers with BMI 23.0-24.9 kg/m2 and its association with birth outcomes, overall and by Asian subgroup, and to compare Asian and White mothers. Methods: Repeated cross-sectional study of US singleton live births, 2016-2023 (National Vital Statistics System). Outcomes were hypertensive disorders, caesarean delivery, preterm birth, and low birthweight. Modified Poisson regression, adjusted for confounders and Asian subgroup, estimated risk ratios (RRs), standardized risks, and risk differences (RDs). We tested for a change in slope at 23.0 kg/m2, subgroup heterogeneity, and race x BMI interaction. Results: Among 1,758,116 non-Hispanic Asian mothers, 314,510 (17.9%) had BMI 23.0-24.9 kg/m2, 30.4% of normal-weight mothers. Compared with BMI 18.5-22.9, standardized risk of hypertensive disorders was 4.5% versus 3.2% (RD 1.4 percentage points, 95% CI 1.3, 1.5; RR 1.44, 95% CI 1.40, 1.47), and of caesarean delivery 32.4% versus 28.6% (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.13, 1.14). Preterm birth risk was 7.2% versus 6.6% (RR 1.08, 95% CI 1.06, 1.10); low birthweight risk was not higher (7.1% versus 7.5%; RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.93, 0.97). The hypertensive-disorder slope showed no evidence of change at 23.0 (ratio of per-unit RRs 0.99, 95% CI 0.98, 1.01); the hypertensive-disorder RR ranged from 1.24 (95% CI 1.18, 1.29) among Asian Indian to 1.70 (95% CI 1.60, 1.81) among Chinese mothers. BMI-outcome associations differed between Asian and White mothers. Conclusions: Nearly one in three normal-weight Asian mothers had BMI 23.0-24.9 kg/m2, associated with higher risks of hypertensive disorders and caesarean delivery but not low birthweight. The hypertensive-disorder gradient showed no evidence of change at 23.0 kg/m2, and associations varied across Asian subgroups.

after.authors: Peng, X.; Chen, Z.; Jia, P.; Zhang, C.; Zhang, M.; Zhong, Y.; Sun, A.; Huang, S.; Li, W.; Zhang, X.; Cai, J.; Liu, Z.; Luo, J.; Su, J.; Sun, C.; Yu, Q.; Tan, Q.; Zheng, Z.; Zou, L.; He, J.; Li, B.; Faria, N. R.; Yu, H.
after.abstract: In 2025, a chikungunya outbreak in southern China resulted in more than 25,000 confirmed cases, but its origins and transmission history remain unresolved. As part of the public health investigation, we generated 1,264 near-complete chikungunya virus (CHIKV) genomes from Guangdong Province and integrated genomic, epidemiological, entomological, and human mobility data to reconstruct the emergence and spread of this outbreak. Our analyses traced the outbreak to a single dominant introduction of a Reunion-associated East/Central/South African (ECSA) virus lineage and dated the origin of the sampled Guangdong outbreak lineage from late April to early May 2025. The interval between the estimated origin of the outbreak lineage and the first reported case was consistent with a period of undetected local transmission and exposed limitations in passive surveillance for early arboviral outbreak detection. Spatiotemporal reconstruction showed two distinct epidemic waves with contrasting transmission dynamics. The Foshan wave involved frequent medium- to long-distance viral movement, while the Jiangmen wave remained relatively localized. Together, these findings reconstruct the early establishment and spatially heterogeneous spread of the largest documented CHIKV epidemic in southern China to date and demonstrate the necessity of expanding active genomic surveillance in areas at the fringe of CHIKV endemic transmission for timely detecting and characterizing emerging epidemics.

after.abstract: Importance: Severe anorexia nervosa (AN) carries substantial mortality risk, but its consequences associated with social and occupational functioning remain poorly characterized, limiting the development of targeted interventions to improve functioning, prevent and reduce long-term social disadvantage. Objective: To determine whether AN severity is associated with educational attainment, employment, income, and cohabitation status. Design: Cohort study following social and occupational outcomes across adulthood until age 55. Setting: Population-based. Participants: All individuals born in Denmark from 1963 to 1994, alive and residing in Denmark at age 30. The AN group had a first AN diagnosis between ages 10 and 25 years, excluding those who died or emigrated within 5 years. The comparison group had no AN diagnosis. Exposure: Illness severity of AN, measured by the AN Register-based Severity Index 5 years after the first AN diagnosis. Main Outcomes and Measures: Educational attainment was assessed at age 25 (upper secondary education) and at age 30/35 (highest completed education). Employment status, income deficiency, and cohabitation status were assessed annually from age 30 to 55. Results: Among 2,442,916 individuals, 9,465 were diagnosed with AN, of whom 1,996 (21.1%) were classified as severe AN cases. At age 25, individuals with severe AN had increased odds of non-completion of upper-secondary education compared to the general population (odds ratio [OR]=3.07; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.72-3.46), and those with less severe AN (OR=1.39; 95% CI: 1.29-1.50). At age 30, severe AN was associated with higher odds of unemployment (OR=3.42; 95% CI: 3.03-3.86), income deficiency (OR=3.84; 95% CI: 3.42-4.31), and living alone (OR=2.43; 95% CI: 2.17-2.71) compared to the less severe AN group. The risk of unemployment and income deficiency diverged across time: individuals with less severe AN gradually approached the general population, whereas those with severe AN diverged further over time. Within the AN cohort, severity differences persisted after adjustment for active AN diagnosis, with minimal attenuation. Conclusions and Relevance: Greater lifetime AN severity was associated with significantly poorer long-term social and occupational functioning outcomes, and these functional difficulties may persist beyond periods of active illness. This vulnerable group needs substantial support in these areas throughout the course of illness.

after.title: Preprint: Classical machine learning versus transformers for predicting daily psychological distress from passive smartphone sensing and self-report: a prospective cohort study
after.authors: Griss Salas, I.; Lam, W.-Y.; Kilshaw, R. E.; Baucom, B. R. W.; de Lacy, N.
after.abstract: Objective: We test whether data collected from daily passive smartphone sensing and self-reports can predict daily significant psychological distress with meaningful potential clinical utility, comparing across best-in-class machine learning algorithms. Methods: In this prospective cohort study, 169 community-dwelling adults completed baseline surveys followed by 7 days of passive smartphone sensing (accelerometer, GPS, power state) and end-of-day Brief Symptom Inventory-18 (BSI-18) assessments. Cases were defined as days (total n = 1,062) where participants' psychological distress measured with the sex-specific BSI-18 Global Severity Index T-score was [≥]63 (prevalence 11.2%). Four classical models (artificial neural network, elastic net, support vector machine [SVM], extreme gradient boosting [XGB]) and four transformers (sensor-only or multimodal; standard or fusion architecture) were tuned, Platt-calibrated and evaluated on held-out participants (210 records, 25 cases) with participant-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: The SVM (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.84; 95% CI 0.71-0.93), the multimodal fusion transformer (0.84; 0.69-0.95) and XGB (0.82; 0.63-0.94) discriminated best; sensor-only transformers performed at chance (0.49-0.50). At the default threshold of 0.50, elastic net logistic regression was the best classifier (sensitivity 0.56, positive predictive value 0.64). At 0.12 (near the outcome prevalence), the SVM detected all cases (negative predictive value 1.00), but positive predictive values were low for all models (0.13-0.26). Decision-curve analysis favored most models over treat-all and treat-none lines at thresholds between 0.05 and 0.25. Baseline survey items, mainly on functional impairment, had the largest feature importance. Conclusions: Compact classical models performed as well as transformers, which were considerably more computationally intensive. Decision-curve analysis supports further clinical exploration of these tools for triaging daily psychological distress, though our results suggest the relative value of psychosocial assessments and digital data should be carefully analyzed. External validation is needed before clinical use.

after.title: Preprint: Balancing Analgesic Effects and Abuse Liability in Older Adults: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial of Oral and Vaporized Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol
after.authors: Costa, G. P. A.; Gueorguieva, R.; Riggs, M. M.; Dunlap, T.; Sofuoglu, M.; De Aquino, J. P.
after.abstract: Cannabis use is rising fastest among older adults in the U.S., and pain is among the most common reasons they use it. No trial, however, has measured the trade-off between the analgesic and abuse-related effects of {Delta}9-tetrahydrocannabinol ({Delta}9-THC) in this population. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 20 adults aged 65 and older were assigned to oral {Delta}9-THC (placebo, 5, 10 mg) or vaporized {Delta}9-THC (placebo, 2, 4 mg) across three eight-hour sessions in counterbalanced order. We assessed laboratory-evoked pain sensitivity using quantitative sensory testing, abuse liability using subjective drug effects and reinforcement value, and also sampled plasma {Delta}9-THC and 11-OH-THC. Analgesia and abuse liability outcomes were measured repeatedly within each session. On a pain sensitivity index, oral 5 mg relieved pain relative to placebo (p=.040), although the oral arms overall dose effect was not significant (p=.108); oral 10 mg and both vaporized doses did not differ from placebo. Subjective effects increased with dose and were greatest after vaporization, whereas reinforcement value increased only after vaporized 4 mg. After oral 5 mg, analgesia exceeded placebo at every assessment (60-360 min), while its pleasurable effects peaked at 150 min. Vaporized {Delta}9-THC produced pleasurable effects within 30 min but did not significantly change thermal pain sensitivity. While abuse liability tracked {Delta}9-THC exposure, analgesia showed no significant association, and all adverse events occurred at vaporized 4 mg. These findings suggest dose and route selection may help maximize {Delta}9-THC analgesia while minimizing abuse liability, a strategy that warrants evaluation in clinical populations.

after.title: Preprint: Understanding, Confidence and Usefulness of Effect Size and Certainty of Evidence: A Cross-Sectional Survey Among Australian Dietitians
after.authors: Ghosh, N. R.; Neale, E. P.; Johnston, B. C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Nutrition, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA; Department of Surgery, Houston Methodist H
after.abstract:
PurposeInterpreting treatment effect size is essential for evidence-sinformed dietetic care, yet dietitians understanding remains unestablished.

MethodsWe conducted a web-based cross-sectional survey of Australian dietitians (October 2024-February 2025). The survey assessed their understanding of effect size, presented using three absolute estimates (risk difference [RD], risk in treatment vs. risk in control groups, number needed to treat [NNT]) and two relative estimates (relative risk [RR], odds ratio [OR]). We also assessed dietitians confidence in determining correct effect size, their perceived usefulness of effect estimates and corresponding certainty of evidence.

ResultsApproximately 7,697 dietitians received the survey link; 27 participated and 13 completers were analyzed. Correct understanding was higher for absolute than relative estimates (30.0% vs. 18.2%). Risk in treatment vs. risk in control groups was understood the most (41.7%) and RD, RR and OR the least (18.2% each). Confidence was highest for RR [mean (SD): 4.18 (1.25)] and lowest for NNT [3.40 (1.17)]. Perceived usefulness was highest for OR [4.69 (1.18)] and lowest for NNT [3.75 (1.76)]. Certainty of evidence was rated useful [5.69 (1.03)].

ConclusionBased on a small sample, preliminary evidence suggests limited understanding of effect size, highlighting the need for further training and assessment in larger sample.

after.title: Preprint: Clinical and Social Determinants of Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy Optimization in Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction
after.authors: Nelson, M.; Kwon, M.; Driscoll, K.; Kaiwan, O.; Dunlap, M. E.; Murad, K.; Rybinska- Campbel, A.; Gunzler, D. D.; Nandar, P. P.
after.abstract:
BackgroundHeart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is associated with high morbidity and mortality. Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) for HFrEF has been shown to improve outcomes, with higher GDMT scores at hospital discharge being associated with lower mortality, fewer rehospitalizations and reduced healthcare costs. Yet, disparities in the utilization of GDMT remain. In this study, we examined the effect of various clinical, demographic, and socioeconomic factors on the utilization of GDMT in HFrEF patients referred to Cardiology in a tertiary care safety net hospital, using a standardized GDMT scoring system.

MethodsWe conducted a single-center cross-sectional retrospective analysis of patients who had an index HFrEF [≤] 40% diagnosis between January 1, 2024, to December 31, 2024, and who were referred to Cardiology at a tertiary care safety net hospital. Baseline characteristics, laboratory investigations, health care utilization, and GDMT score data were extracted at the ambulatory care visit nearest to 90 days from the index HF diagnosis. GDMT score ranges from 0 to 9 factored in doses of beta-blocker (BB), angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor/angiotensin receptor blocker (ACEi/ARB), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA), sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i), angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), isosorbide dinitrate/hydralazine (ISDN/HYD). Multivariable logistic regression was performed to examine associations between low GDMT scores (0-4) nearest to 90 days from new onset HFrEF diagnosis and several clinical, demographic, and socioeconomic variables.

ResultsIn 200 patients meeting entry criteria, mean age was 62.7 years, 64.0% were male, 47.5% were classified as white and 42.0% as Black. 39.5% had a low GDTM score (<5). The following were less likely to be associated with low GDMT score: diabetes mellitus (adjusted OR: 0.41, 95%CI=0.18-0.91) and frequent medical appointments (adjusted OR: 0.37, 95% CI=0.25-0.54), while higher serum eGFR was more likely to be associated with low GDMT score (adjusted OR: 1.02, 95%CI=1.00-1.03). There was no significant association between GDMT score and age, sex, race, or payer status.

ConclusionIn patients with HFrEF referred to Cardiology in our safety net tertiary care center, higher utilization of GDMT at 90 days was achieved in those who have diabetes mellitus, more frequent medical appointments, or lower serum eGFR. There was no difference in GDMT utilization according to age, sex, race, or payer status predictive of lower GDMT scores. Contrary to findings from previous studies, no significant differences were observed across demographic or payer groups, emphasizing the role of healthcare access and utilization.

data.summary: added: Preprint: The origin of the MV Hondius Andes outbreak

after.title: Preprint: The origin of the MV Hondius Andes outbreak
after.authors: Ulloa-Zepeda, L.; Parker, E.; Gangavarapu, K.; Castillo, A.; Pavez, C.; Fernandez, J.; Vilches, M.; Vial, P.; Rambaut, A.; Andersen, K. G.; Vial, C.
after.abstract: In April-July 2026, Andes virus (ANDV) caused an outbreak aboard the MV Hondius cruise ship resulting in 12 confirmed cases and three deaths. Before symptom onset, the index case had travelled through hantavirus-endemic regions of Chile and Argentina, leaving the geographic origin of infection unresolved. We conducted phylogenetic and phylogeographic analyses using newly generated ANDV genomes from human cases and rodent reservoirs to investigate the likely origin of the outbreak. Through phylogenetic analyses, we show that the outbreak genome falls within a geographically structured lineage spanning southern Chile and Argentine Andean Patagonia. Using phylogeographic reconstructions across all three segments, integrated with the index cases travel itinerary, we identified the Tolten-Lanco area of southern Chile as the most likely geographic origin of the outbreak genome, with two candidate locations accounting for >98% of the posterior support. However, the index case visited this area 62-66 days before symptom onset, exceeding the conventionally reported ANDV incubation period of 7-42 days. Thus, while genomic evidence supports a southern Chilean origin of the outbreak genome, the timing and circumstances of transmission to the index case remain unresolved.

after.title: Preprint: Spatial distribution and factors associated with unmet need for family planning among women of reproductive age in Zambia: Evidence from the 2024 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey
after.authors: Sibeso, P.; Tembo, N.; Jacobs, C.
after.abstract: Unmet need for family planning contributes to unintended pregnancies, unsafe abortions, and preventable maternal and child deaths, and remains high in sub-Saharan Africa. In Zambia, national estimates may conceal important geographic inequalities. We assessed the spatial distribution of unmet need for family planning among women of reproductive age in Zambia and the factors associated with it. We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of the 2024 Zambia Demographic and Health Survey (ZDHS), including 12,133 women aged 15-49 years. We used survey-weighted logistic regression, accounting for the stratified two-stage cluster design, to estimate adjusted odds ratios (AOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Global spatial autocorrelation was assessed with Morans I, local hotspots with the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic, and spatial clusters with a purely spatial Bernoulli scan statistic in SaTScan. The weighted prevalence of unmet need was 27.0% (95% CI: 25.7-28.3%), ranging from 23.8% in Central to 31.6% in North-Western Province. Unmet need was spatially clustered (Morans I = 0.142, p = 0.018), with hotspots mainly in Lusaka, Southern, North-Western, and Northern provinces; SaTScan detected a primary cluster in Lusaka (observed-to-expected ratio 1.42, p < 0.001). Women in union (AOR 2.33, 95% CI: 1.90-2.86) and never-married women (AOR 2.20, 95% CI: 1.69-2.86) had higher odds of unmet need than formerly married women, as did women with five or more children compared with none (AOR 3.05, 95% CI: 2.25-4.13). Lower odds were observed among women aged 35-49 years (AOR 0.65, 95% CI: 0.52-0.83), women in the richest wealth quintile (AOR 0.62, 95% CI: 0.45-0.86), employed women (AOR 0.73, 95% CI: 0.64-0.84) and urban residents (AOR 0.80, 95% CI: 0.68-0.95). Unmet need for family planning in Zambia is high, geographically clustered and socially patterned. Family planning programmes should prioritise hotspot areas, particularly Lusaka, Southern and North-Western provinces, while targeting younger, higher-parity and poorer women.

Lower odds were observed among women aged 35-49 years (AOR 0.65, 95% CI: 0.52-0.83), women in the richest wealth quintile (AOR 0.62, 95% CI: 0.45-0.86), employed women (AOR 0.73, 95% CI: 0.64-0.84) and urban residents (AOR 0.80, 95% CI: 0.68-0.95). after.authors: Taylor-Egbeyemi, J. L.; Masterton, S.; Robin, C.
after.abstract:
BackgroundTicks in the UK can transmit pathogens that lead to diseases in humans, including Lyme disease and tick-borne encephalitis. Expanding tick populations and increasing human use of urban green spaces may elevate exposure risk. Public health advice exists, but little is known about how this guidance is understood and applied by users of urban environments.

MethodsFour stakeholder focus groups were conducted with professionals involved in tick fieldwork in urban green spaces. Discussions explored interactions with the public, perceived awareness, behaviours, and views on communication. Data were analysed thematically using an approach informed by the Framework Method.

ResultsStakeholders reported substantial variation in public awareness of ticks, influenced by prior exposure to rural environments and local knowledge. Misinformation, particularly around tick removal, was common. Signage was rarely observed in urban green spaces, and views on its effectiveness were mixed. Participants emphasised the need to balance risk communication with reassurance and highlighted the importance of age-appropriate education.

ConclusionsInsights from stakeholders underline the importance of targeted, context-specific public health messaging in urban settings. Priorities include identifying groups with lower awareness, addressing misinformation, designing balanced communication materials, evaluating the effectiveness of signage, and integrating education for children and families.

after.title: Preprint: Effects of Weighted Seated Core Exercises on Immediate Postural Stability in Healthy Young Adults: An Exploratory Study
after.authors: Fujino, F.; Yamakawa, M.; Kono, T.; Higaki, T.; Maeda, K.
after.abstract:
ObjectivesThis exploratory study investigated whether low-load, seated core exercises could produce immediate improvements in standing balance among healthy young adults, aiming to provide a foundation for safe, early-stage rehabilitation protocols.

MethodsTen healthy males performed seated core exercises consisted of alternating hip flexion 5 times per side while seated and maintaining bilateral shoulder flexion at 120{degrees} shoulder flexion under four load conditions: upper-limb weight only, a 400-g empty box, a 1-kg ball, and a 2-kg ball. Immediately following the exercise, participants performed a 10-s single-leg stance. Transversus abdominis (TrA) thickness was measured via wireless ultrasound at baseline, post-exercise, and during the stance. Center of pressure (CoP) sway was recorded concurrently to evaluate postural stability.

ResultsLeft-side TrA thickness during stance increased significantly under the 1-kg and 2-kg load conditions compared to baseline (p < 0.05), although substantial missing data for the left-side measurements limited the robustness of this finding. No significant load-dependent effects were observed for CoP sway parameters (p > 0.05). A moderate positive correlation ({rho} = 0.43, p = 0.002) was found between right-side TrA thickness and CoP sway velocity during the single-leg stance.

ConclusionsLow-load, seated core exercises do not yield immediate enhancements in standing stability in healthy populations. The results suggest that increased TrA thickness during a balance task may correlate with heightened postural instability rather than improved balance control. Further research is needed to determine whether these findings translate to clinical populations with impaired physical fitness.

after.authors: Shahani, J.; Ousta, A. R.; Shaulov, S.; El-Sherif, Y.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, Staten Island University Hospital, Northwell Health, Staten Island, NY, USA; Zucker School of Medicine at Hofstra/Northwell, Hempstead,
after.abstract:
ObjectiveTo develop and independently validate a decomposed, modality-specific large language model (LLM) pipeline that abstracts structured variables from the free-text neuroimaging reports of a multimodal stroke workup, and to validate the resulting structured dataset for reuse in downstream research.

Materials and MethodsA frozen pipeline (temperature 0) extracting 22 variables across CT head, CT angiography, CT perfusion, and MRI brain was applied to 1,669 ED encounters for dizziness or vertigo; 11 variables were pre-specified as primary (Tier 1). Reproducibility used three same-session runs and a nine-week re-run; three frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.5 Flash) measured cross-model agreement (Cohens/Fleiss {kappa}). Accuracy was assessed in an independent 200-encounter cohort (150 random, 50 enriched for rare findings); 100 were double-read by two blinded reviewers with discordances adjudicated.

ResultsTest-retest reproducibility was high (Tier 1 Fleiss {kappa}=0.993; 99.8% exact) and stable nine weeks later ({kappa}=0.992); inter-model agreement was {kappa}=0.962. Against the adjudicated reference, pooled Tier 1 accuracy was 0.971 to 0.988 across models (Cohens {kappa} 0.959 to 0.982), comparable to inter-reviewer agreement ({kappa}=0.932). Accuracy was 0.980 to 0.983 in random and 0.955 to 0.977 in enriched encounters (agreement on model-flagged findings, not sensitivity).

DiscussionA decomposed LLM pipeline produced reproducible, model-portable, stable, and accurate multimodal abstraction. Because schema design and validation are up-front costs, such pipelines scale to larger research cohorts.

ConclusionThe quantified per-field error rates support reuse of this dataset with field-specific review, and such pipelines offer a practical path to large-scale, reproducible research datasets.

after.authors: Sunuwar, D. R.; Shrestha, A.; Kiwanayo, A.; Karki, S.; Shrestha, M.; Sunuwar, S.; Singh, D. R.; Karki, K.; Chaudhary, N. K.; K.C., D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Public Health Promotion and Development Organization
after.abstract:
BackgroundThe double burden of malnutrition (DBM), characterised by coexisting undernutrition and overnutrition, remains a public health concern among adolescents especially in low- and middle-income countries. Adolescents in Nepal are nutritionally vulnerable, yet evidence on the coexistence of stunting and overweight/obesity is limited. This study assessed the prevalence and associated factors of DBM among school-going adolescents in urban Kathmandu Valley, Nepal.

MethodsA school-based cross-sectional study was conducted to assess factors associated with the double burden of malnutrition among adolescents in Kathmandu Valley, Nepal from 25th April, 2022 up to 25th July, 2025. A multi-stage cluster random sampling technique, using the Probability Proportional to Size method, was employed to ensure the selection of the desired number of participants. Students from grades 8 to 10 were randomly selected for face-to-face interviews and anthropometric measurements (height and weight were collected to calculate Body Mass Index (BMI)-for-age Z-scores (BAZ)), using tools adapted to the local context. Bivariate and multivariable models examined the associations between the dependent and independent variables.

ResultsThis study revealed that 15.3% of the students were stunted, 5.5% were underweight, 16.9% were overweight/obese, and 3% of students with the coexistence of DBM.

In the fully adjusted model, the odds of stunting were significantly higher among adolescents aged 15-19 years (aOR = 2.03, 95% CI: 1.35-3.06), salty-snack consumers (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.00-2.36), those with low nutritional knowledge (aOR = 3.17, 95% CI: 2.17-4.66), and low diet quality (aOR = 7.27, 95% CI: 4.96-10.65). Conversely, fatty-food consumption was associated with lower odds of stunting (aOR = 0.65, 95% CI: 0.42-1.00). For overweight/obesity, older adolescents had significantly lower odds (aOR = 0.49, 95% CI: 0.35-0.67). Regarding the double burden of malnutrition (DBM), low nutritional knowledge (aOR = 2.16, 95% CI: 0.99-4.71) and low diet quality (aOR = 5.27, 95% CI: 2.42-11.48) were significantly associated with higher odds.

ConclusionThe double burden of malnutrition exists among adolescents in urban Kathmandu Valley, highlighting a critical public health challenge. Socio-demographic, dietary, and behavioral factors significantly influence its prevalence. Comprehensive school- and community-based interventions are crucial for addressing this dual nutritional burden.

after.abstract: Immune allele frequencies inform disease association mapping, pharmacogenomic guidance, and vaccine design, yet such data are missing for most of the worlds groups. Here we present the Global Atlas of Immune Alleles (GAIA), applying benchmarked genotyping tools across the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA), Immunoglobulin Heavy Chain Constant (IGHC), and Fc Gamma Receptor (FCGR) loci to whole-genome sequencing data from 20,248 individuals, oversampling sub-Saharan African, Island Southeast Asian, and Pacific groups. Despite representing fewer than 0.5% of observations in the Allele Frequency Net Database, GAIA expands the databases catalogue by 38%, demonstrating that representation matters more than sample size. We identify HLA alleles at group-specific frequencies that challenge pharmacogenomic screening recommendations and document disease-risk alleles common in groups lacking clinical guidance. Finally, we introduce majority allelic diversity (MAD-X), which counts the alleles required for X% of individuals in a group to carry at least one, and show that reaching 90% HLA-B coverage for vaccine design requires up to 2.7 times more alleles in underrepresented groups than in those of Northwest European ancestry.

after.authors: Yarnell, C. J.; Bruce-Kemevor, S.; Burns, K.; Burry, L.; Craig, J.; Fernando, S. M.; Fowler, R.; Gunaratne, K.; Haskings, J.; Lamontagne, F.; Liu, K.; Prakash, V.; Sibley, S.; Soliman, K.; Tomlinson, G.; Wei, L.; Bodley, T.; Canadian Critical Care Trials Group,
after.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
after.abstract:
Abstract {1b}O_ST_ABSBackgroundC_ST_ABSMeasurement of serum magnesium levels, and administration of supplemental magnesium when levels are below target, is a common element of routine care for critically ill patients. However, targets for replacement vary, and the targets that lead to the best outcomes are unknown.

MethodsMulti-center open-label parallel group randomized controlled superiority trial of adult critically ill patients receiving protocolized magnesium replacement, comparing a higher target (>0.95mmol/L) to a lower target (>0.7mmol/L). The trial will be embedded into the electronic health record (EHR) at 6 hospitals across 2 health networks in Ontario, Canada, with a shared EHR. We will include patients aged 16 years or older who have ICU admission orders, including an order for the magnesium replacement protocol. Patients with pre-eclampsia, sustained ventricular tachycardia, or neuromuscular junction disease will be excluded. Because both targets lie within the standard of care, we will use an opt-out consent approach. Screening will be integrated with the EHR, such that when a patient meets inclusion criteria, a pop-up will appear to allow the ordering clinician to confirm eligibility or indicate the relevant exclusion. After the clinician confirms eligibility, patients will be randomly assigned to a magnesium target. The primary outcome will be an ordinal composite, evaluated at 30 days, composed of death and the number of days free of atrial fibrillation or flutter in ICU. Secondary outcomes will include ventricular arrhythmia and antiarrhythmics administered; receipt of vasopressors, ventilation, and new renal replacement therapy in ICU; lengths of ICU and hospital stay; hospital mortality at 60 and 90 days, magnesium levels, and magnesium supplementation. For analyses, we will use Bayesian regression with weakly skeptical priors and an intention-to-treat approach. Outcome ascertainment will occur within the EHR.

DiscussionThis randomized controlled trial addresses an important uncertainty regarding routine care in the ICU with an EHR-embedded design. The innovative EHR-embedded design facilitates the large sample sizes and comprehensive, equitable recruitment needed for a trial evaluating a routine care intervention, and will lead to seamless integration with routine care upon trial completion.

Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov, NCT07173855. Registered 12 September 2025, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07173855.

after.abstract: BACKGROUND Risk models from high-income transplant programmes may not generalise to resource-constrained settings with different recipient acuity, donor characteristics and access to mechanical circulatory support. We developed RIGHT-HTx, a parsimonious framework integrating clinical and physiological vulnerabilities, and evaluated its prognostic performance in a subsequent same-centre cohort. METHODS This retrospective single-centre study included 436 consecutive adult heart transplant recipients (2012-2026). Of 357 development recipients, 341 (95.5%) were score-evaluable. RIGHT-HTx incorporated three vulnerability domains: clinical acuity (INTERMACS 1-2), graded renal dysfunction (eGFR 30-59 or <30 mL/min/1.73 m2) and haemodynamic-donor mismatch (TPG >12 mmHg combined with donor-to-recipient weight ratio <1.0). after.authors: Cromie, A.; Kaur, M.; Powell, N.; Brown, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Swansea University College of Medicine: Swansea University Medical School
after.abstract: Background Medical professionals face significant work overload, with excessive job demands often strongly associated with attrition and burnout. Consequences of burnout include reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, reduced patient care, lower patient satisfaction and increased healthcare costs. UK Medical students are also at high risk of burnout. Mindfulness-based interventions are effective individual-level treatments, however more research is required to investigate the efficacy of mindfulness for healthcare professionals and students.   Method Four cohorts of second-year medical students at Cardiff University participated in a five-day, in-person mindfulness-based intervention. Pre (T1) and post (T2) intervention and follow-up (T3) survey data were collected online using validated outcome measures for burnout, psychological distress and wellbeing. Results Statistical analysis of data from 69 participants found a statistically significant improvement post intervention (T2) for current energy, calmness, focus and stress (all P=0.001). Statistically significant improvements in psychological distress (Core-10, P=0.001), Burnout (OLBI, P=0.023), and Wellbeing (WHO5, P=0.37) with small, large and small effect sizes respectively; maintained at follow-up (T3). Satisfaction ratings were consistently high, and completion rate was 100%. Discussion Medical schools should consider implementing mindfulness-based interventions into medical curricula, as a feasible and acceptable student selected preventative tool to address burnout and incorporate student perspectives on delivery; to prevent mental ill health in medical professionals.

after.abstract: Background: Contemporary data on long-term, cause-specific mortality among stroke survivors are sparse, and much of the existing evidence derives from studies performed before the modern reperfusion era. We sought to characterize long-term cause-specific mortality among stroke survivors to discharge (differentiated by stroke subtype) when compared to in-hospital stroke decedents treated under contemporary standards of care. Methods: Using a hybrid billing-code/imaging and large language model-assisted chart-review pipeline, we identified adults hospitalized for ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke in the Observational Study of Cardiac Arrest Risk (OSCAR) cohort (Cedars-Sinai Health System, Los Angeles) between 2017 and 2020, followed through June 30, 2025. Cause of death was determined and classified into 10 categories. Results: Among 1,344 stroke patients (mean age 74.0 {+/-} 14.9 years; ischemic n=1,036 [77.1%], hemorrhagic n=308 [22.9%]), 203 (15.1%) did not survive the index stroke. Of the 1,141 discharged survivors, 625 (54.8%) died over a median follow-up of 5.2 years. Cerebrovascular causes predominated during index stroke hospitalization (36.0%) but accounted for only 15.5% of post-stroke discharge deaths. Among ischemic stroke survivors, cardiac disease was the leading cause of death (31.6%), with sudden cardiac arrest alone accounting for 10.9% of deaths. Among hemorrhagic stroke survivors, cancer (38.9%) was the leading cause of death. Despite these divergent cause-of-death profiles, overall survival did not differ significantly by subtype (median 5.5 vs 5.8 years; P=0.90). Conclusions: In this contemporary, reperfusion-era cohort, causes of death shifted from cerebrovascular predominance in the acute phase to heart disease/cardiac arrest after ischemic stroke, and malignancy after hemorrhagic stroke. These findings argue for development of subtype-specific post-stroke surveillance, including structured longitudinal cardiac and sudden-death risk assessment for ischemic stroke survivors.

after.abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid-{beta} plaques and neurofibrillary tangles of tau. Suvorexant, a dual orexin receptor antagonist, was previously shown to acutely reduce the ratio of phosphorylated tau-181 to unphosphorylated tau-181 (pT181/T181) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). However, its effects on plasma pT181/T181 and broader proteomic networks remain unknown. Here, we conducted a secondary analysis of samples from a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 25 participants receiving placebo or suvorexant 20 mg. Paired CSF and plasma samples were collected longitudinally via indwelling intrathecal and intravenous catheters. Plasma AD biomarkers were quantified by mass spectrometry, and proteomic profiling was performed using the SomaScan 11K assay on samples from hours 0, 16, and 24. Suvorexant increased pT181/T181 in plasma while decreasing it in CSF between 08:00 to 16:00. At the pathway level, suvorexant increased the extracellular abundance of proteins associated with translation, RNA binding, cytoskeletal organization and endosomal sorting, centrally at 16 hours and peripherally at 24 hours, and decreased cytokine and receptor-ligand signaling and serine protease activity in plasma at 24 hours. As plasma biomarkers are increasingly used for clinical screening and trial enrollment, factors that influence their levels, including medications, must be identified and their effects on interpretation understood.

after.abstract: Background: Altered memory self-awareness is common in mild cognitive impairment (MCI), but its relationship to Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology and progression remains unclear. Methods: Using 590 amnestic MCI ADNI participants, memory self-awareness was derived from participant-informant discrepancies on the memory subdomain of the Everyday Cognition questionnaire. Heightened awareness and unawareness subscores were calculated, and k-means clustering identified four phenotypes. Associations with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and positron emission tomography (PET) were examined, and clinical progression was assessed using Cox models. Results: Aware and Unaware groups showed lower CSF amyloid-B, and higher CSF phosphorylated tau and PET amyloid. The Unaware phenotype was associated with increased progression risk (hazard ratio 2.41, 95% CI 1.48-3.92), whereas the Worried Well phenotype showed reduced risk (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.34-0.99). Conclusions: Multidimensional assessment of memory self-awareness identifies biologically and prognostically distinct subgroups within MCI and may improve risk stratification in prodromal AD.

after.abstract: Purpose Germline shelterin variants were linked to sarcoma in a case-enriched cohort. Whether shelterin loss of function predisposes to mesenchymal neoplasia in the general population is unknown. Methods We analyzed rare-variant collapsing associations for five shelterin genes across neoplasm phenotypes in UK Biobank exomes, with Genebass as a second pipeline. Prespecified shelterin and centrosome gene sets were tested by permutation-calibrated statistics against a TP53/RB1/NF1 positive control. Carrier risks were compared with telomere-lengthening predictions. Results Lipoma risk was increased in TERF1 (odds ratio [OR], 3.32; P = 8.4 x10-), POT1, and TERF2IP carriers, and uterine leiomyoma risk in all four core shelterin genes, most strongly POT1 (OR, 2.23; P = 4.0 x 10-); POT1 and TINF2 reproduced in Genebass. TERF1 was also associated with thyroid cancer and monoclonal gammopathy. Neither gene set nor the positive control was associated with self-reported sarcoma. Telomere lengthening accounted for POT1-associated chronic lymphocytic leukemia risk but not myeloma or TINF2-associated thyroid cancer, where observed risk exceeded prediction five- to seven-fold. Conclusion Shelterin loss of function is a population-level risk factor for lipoma and uterine leiomyoma, the benign counterparts of liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma. TERF1 joins POT1 and TINF2 as long-telomere cancer genes. Sarcoma-specific penetrance remains untested.

after.abstract: Short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (ECHS1) catalyzes the hydration of C4-C6 acyl-CoA molecules to produce ATP in fatty acid {beta}-oxidation. Deficiency of the ECHS1 enzyme, ECHS1D, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that presents with a large and pleomorphic clinical spectrum. We present the largest comprehensive study of known diagnosed ECHS1D patients to date, reporting 26 new patients and 8 novel variants in conjunction with a literature review of 87 previously reported patients. All patients were categorized into neonatal, infantile, and late-onset groups based on age of onset and clinical course. Neonatal-onset cases were characterized by early and severe multisystem disease, often with lactic acidosis, hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, and high early mortality (62.5%). The infantile-onset group was heterogeneous, but many exhibited hallmark features such as dystonia, developmental delay, and basal ganglia involvement on neuroimaging. Mortality was significantly lower than the neonatal cohort (24.4%). Late-onset patients had more localized neurologic symptoms, particularly dystonia, and significantly lower mortality overall (0%). Moreover, we report a 37.5% survival rate in newly reported neonatal onset patients compared with 18.2% in prior reports, possibly reflective of earlier recognition of ECHS1D and greater utilization of therapies including N-acetylcysteine, sodium dichloroacetate, and valine-restricted diet.

after.title: Preprint: Application of Machine Learning and Deep Learning in diagnosis Covid19
after.authors: Merchi, L.; Boucheham, C.; Layeb, A.; Derouiche, A.
after.abstract: Predicting the progression of COVID-19 in hospitalised patients was an important challenge during the pandemic, particularly when healthcare resources were limited. This study investigates the use of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models to predict three clinical outcomes: death, admission to the intensive care unit (ICU), and clinical status (improvement or worsening). The study uses two patient datasets: an Algerian cohort of 80 patients from the Internal Medicine Department of the University Hospital Centre of Constantine, collected between July and August 2020, and a French cohort of 99 patients collected between March and May 2020. Five ML classifiers were evaluated: logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbours (KNN), classification and regression trees (CART), Naive Bayes (NB), and support vector machines (SVM). Their performance was examined in combination with three feature-selection methods: analysis of variance (ANOVA), mutual information (MI), and recursive feature elimination (RFE). The results were also compared with multilayer perceptron (MLP) models using one to five hidden layers. Model evaluation included 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation on the training data, followed by evaluation on a separate hold-out test set. The results showed that selecting 20 features generally provided better cross-validated accuracy than selecting 30 features or using the full feature set. The best-performing classifier-feature-selection combination varied across the six dataset-outcome tasks. LR combined with RFE was selected for three tasks, LR combined with ANOVA for one task, and CART combined with ANOVA for two tasks. The selected ML models achieved test-set accuracies ranging from 0.47 to 0.95 and higher accuracy than the average MLP results in five of the six tasks. These findings suggest that ML methods can be useful for exploring clinical outcomes in hospitalised COVID-19 patients. However, the small sample sizes and limitations of the available data mean that the results should be interpreted with caution. Further evaluation using larger and independent patient datasets is needed before these models can be considered for clinical use.

Model evaluation included 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation on the training data, followed by evaluation on a separate hold-out test set. The results showed that selecting 20 features generally provided better cross-validated accuracy than selecting 30 features or using the full feature set. The best-performing classifier-feature-selection combination varied across the six dataset-outcome tasks. LR combined with RFE was selected for three tasks, LR combined with ANOVA for one task, and CART combined with ANOVA for two tasks. The selected ML models achieved test-set accuracies ranging from 0.47 to 0.95 and higher accuracy than the average MLP results in five of the six tasks. These findings suggest that ML methods can be useful for exploring clinical outcomes in hospitalised COVID-19 patients. However, the small sample sizes and limitations of the available data mean that the results should be interpreted with caution. Further evaluation using larger and independent patient datasets is needed before these models can be considered for clinical use.

after.title: Preprint: Formal dissent in CHMP opinions on new medicines, 2020-2025
after.authors: Siebert, M.; Tibau, A.
after.abstract: Disagreement within medicines regulation is rarely visible in the public record at the point an opinion is adopted. We examined divergent positions formally appended to opinions of the European Medicines Agency's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) on new medicines from 2020 through 2025, both those opposing a positive opinion and those favoring authorization despite a negative opinion, describing how often they occurred, how large the dissenting minorities were, and which issues they raised. Divergent positions opposed 28 of 331 positive opinions (8.5%) and most often concerned efficacy and methodological limitations. Of 22 final negative opinions publicly available, 6 (27%) were accompanied by a divergent position favoring authorization. These records show when CHMP members disagreed about whether the evidence justified authorization. Indexing these disagreements and publishing vote outcomes with each opinion would make regulatory uncertainty visible and help clinicians, payers and health technology assessment bodies make better-informed decisions about treatment use and coverage.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Universite Abdelmalek Essaadi Faculte des Sciences
after.abstract: Drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance requires diagnostic systems that can rapidly identify resistance beyond rifampicin and generate potentially actionable resistance information for routine public-health monitoring. We evaluated programmatic Xpert MTB/XDR use and characterized the molecular resistance profiles generated within a regional tuberculosis diagnostic network in northern Morocco. We retrospectively analyzed 258 Xpert MTB/XDR testing episodes performed from April 2022 to July 2026 and linked available Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra results with target-level molecular outputs. Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex was detected in 203 episodes (78.7%), of which 188 (92.6%) had an interpretable rifampicin result. Molecular rifampicin resistance was detected in 75/188 episodes (39.9%) and isoniazid resistance in 71/192 (37.0%); molecular multidrug-resistant tuberculosis was identified in 51/184 (27.7%) episodes with paired results. Among 186 episodes with interpretable rifampicin and additional resistance results, 75 (40.3%) had resistance to at least one additional drug class, including 21/112 (18.8%) rifampicin-susceptible and 54/74 (73.0%) rifampicin-resistant episodes. Among 92 resistant episodes with complete profiles, 66 (71.7%) showed resistance to two or more drug classes. rpoB3- and rpoB4-associated signals predominated among rifampicin-resistant episodes, katG-associated signals among isoniazid-resistant episodes, and gyrA targets among fluoroquinolone-resistant episodes. Mixed wild-type and mutation-associated signals occurred across rpoB and gyrA. These findings support the use of routine Xpert MTB/XDR testing as a component of regional drug-resistant tuberculosis surveillance, enabling systematic characterization of multiclass resistance and molecular resistance patterns within routine diagnostic networks. Such molecular surveillance should be integrated with phenotypic susceptibility testing and genomic sequencing to resolve discordant, atypical, or clinically consequential profiles and build a more comprehensive regional resistance-monitoring system.

after.abstract: Background: Intensive Care Unit (ICU) mortality remains high among patients with severe coronavirus disease. Static admission severity scores may fail to capture the dynamic clinical trajectory of critically ill patients. We hypothesized that early multiorgan failure (MOF) at 24 hours would improve mortality discrimination beyond admission severity alone. Methods: Retrospective, single-center cohort study of 345 adults with severe COVID-19 pneumonia admitted to a Spanish ICU (March 2020-December 2022). The primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality. Univariate comparisons between survivors and non-survivors were performed, followed by multivariable logistic regression to identify independent predictors of mortality. Three sequential models were constructed and compared by Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC-ROC) discrimination. Results: Overall, in-hospital mortality was 20.6%. Non-survivors were older and had higher Simplified Acute Physiology Score (SAPS) II and Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II scores (p<0.001). MOF at 24 hours was more frequent among non-survivors than survivors (88.4% vs. 61.7%, p<0.001). The baseline model (age, sex, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD), hypertension, and SAPS II) achieved an AUC of 0.798 (95% CI 0.742-0.852). The final model incorporating MOF at 24 hours achieved an AUC of 0.812 (95% CI 0.754-0.860); early MOF nearly tripled the odds of death (OR 2.78, 95% CI 1.22-6.33, p=0.015). Conclusions: Combining baseline severity with early multiorgan dysfunction provides a simple, interpretable approach to mortality risk stratification in critically ill COVID-19 patients; however, external validation is needed before it can inform escalation-of-care or treatment-limitation decisions in clinical practice.

after.authors: Ma, J. R.; Gerges, M.; Koshy, A.; Wilson, W.; Taylor, A.; Chan, W.
after.abstract: Background: Acute decompensated aortic stenosis (ADAS) carries high mortality, but the optimal timing of valve intervention is unknown. Objective: To assess the association between time to valve intervention (transcatheter aortic valve replacement [TAVR] or balloon aortic valvuloplasty [BAV]) and clinical outcomes in ADAS. Methods: Embase, Ovid MEDLINE and CENTRAL were searched to May 15, 2026. Hazard ratios (HRs) for delayed versus earlier intervention were pooled using random-effects models with modified Hartung-Knapp inference. Unadjusted short-term mortality risk ratios (RRs) were pooled using the Mantel-Haenszel method. Results: Eight observational cohort studies (n=6,044) met inclusion criteria: six TAVR (n= 5,986) and two BAV (n=58) studies. Patients were approximately 79 years old, and 63% were male. Early-intervention thresholds ranged from <24-48 hours (BAV) to ?22 days (TAVR) from admission. Delayed intervention was not significantly associated with long-term all-cause mortality (HR 1.52, 95% CI 0.46-5.00; p=0.269; I2=58.2%) or mortality per five-day delay (HR 1.09, 95% CI 0.34-3.43; p=0.530; I2=86.7%). Crude short-term mortality was higher with delayed intervention (RR 4.96, 95% CI 1.17-20.92; p=0.029; I2=0.0%), although this association was not robust to sensitivity analyses. Most studies were at serious risk of bias, with substantial heterogeneity in clinical severity, intervention timing, and treatment modality. Conclusion: Point estimates favour earlier intervention, but current observational data do not establish a mortality benefit for an optimal door-to-valve interval, and existing study designs are biased against early treatment. Prospective and randomized-controlled trials on optimal valve intervention timing following ADAS are needed.

after.authors: Allende-Richter, S.; Stamoulis, C.; Reynier-Hernandez, A.; Brown, C. A.; Pollock, Z. E.; Chiert, H.; Gooding, H. C.; de Ferranti, S. D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Boston Children's Hospital Division of General Pediatrics
after.abstract: Background: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among women, with risk factors commonly emerging during adolescence. Emerging evidence indicates that psychological factors, such as optimism, affect cardiovascular health, yet this remains understudied among young women. To assess the association between overall outlook on life and preventive cardiovascular health behaviors among young women. Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of a cohort of 331 young women aged 15 to 24 years who completed the modified American Heart Association Women?s Health Survey (2017-2018), using multivariate regression adjusted for confounding. Results: Over 50% of young women felt their outlook on life may impact their likelihood of developing a serious illness such as heart disease. Outlook on life was associated with prioritizing and taking care of health (?=0.18-0.19, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) [0.09, 0.29]; P=0.002) and usually following recommended healthy eating (?=0.12, 95% CI [0.03, 0.23]; P=0.016). Young women who identified as black (27.5%; N=91) felt that their outlook on life had a lower impact on their likelihood of developing a serious illness such as heart disease (Odds Ratio (OR)=0.80; 95% CI [0.65, 0.98]; P = 0.04), compared to other racial groups. Conclusion: Our findings support previous observations indicating a cardioprotective role of optimism in cardiovascular health. However, this association may not hold among young women of color, potentially reflecting constraints in their lived environment that limit how much a positive outlook translates into perceived control over health outcomes. Strategies to reduce cardiovascular disease in women should address young women?s cardiovascular health and psychological and contextual factors, with particular attention to young women of color.

after.authors: Tran, B. V.; Chen, C.-L.; Nguyen, T. N.; Lin, Y.-C.; Hu, K.-C.; Hsu, C.-W.; Hsu, S.-C.
after.abstract: Background Sepsis is a dynamic process with evolving host responses, biomarker changes, and organ dysfunction. Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is a bioactive lipid involved in endothelial and immune regulation. However, the clinical relevance of dynamic S1P changes in sepsis remains unclear. This study aimed to assess their association with mortality. Methods We conducted a prospective cohort study of adults recruited from the emergency department of Wan Fang Hospital between April 2022 and October 2024. Plasma S1P was measured by ELISA on days 1, 3, and before discharge or death. The primary outcome was 60-day mortality. S1P trajectories were defined by baseline concentrations and longitudinal slopes estimated using linear mixed-effects models. Low-decreasing, low-stable, and high-decreasing trajectories were grouped as descending; the others as ascending. Cox proportional hazards models assessed mortality associations with baseline S1P, trajectory groups, and time-varying S1P. Results Among 278 participants, 156 had sepsis. Baseline S1P concentrations were lower in patients with sepsis (82.2 [IQR, 47.8-141.1] ng/mL) than in those with non-septic infection (129.2 [IQR, 68.1-306.9] ng/mL) and non-infected controls (132.8 [IQR, 74.1-300.2] ng/mL). In the sepsis cohort, 101 patients were classified into the descending S1P trajectory group and 55 into the ascending group. The descending group had a higher hazard of 60-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 3.43; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.11-10.58; p = 0.032). Baseline S1P was not significantly associated with 60-day mortality (aHR 1.004 per 10 ng/mL decrease; 95% CI, 0.977-1.032; p = 0.803). Each 10 ng/mL decrease in time-varying S1P was associated with a 3.5% higher mortality hazard (aHR 1.035; 95% CI, 1.002-1.076; p = 0.041). Conclusions Declining plasma S1P over time was associated with higher mortality in sepsis. Dynamic changes in S1P may be clinically relevant beyond baseline levels.

after.authors: Reynolds, K. M.; Lash, J.; Morris, A.; Daviglus, M. L.; Gallo, L. C.; Taylor, K. D.; Cai, J.; Cui, J.; Mattix-Kramer, H.; Chen, Y.-D. I.; Sotres-Alvarez, D.; Rotter, J. I. I.; Goodarzi, M. O.; Franceschini, N.

after.abstract: Increased fasting insulin reflects insulin resistance and is as a precursor to type 2 diabetes and a risk factor for kidney, heart and liver diseases and mortality. Cluster-specific fasting insulin polygenic scores (PS) characterize insulin resistance mechanisms based on insulin-related genetic associations with metabolic traits, and they have not been evaluated for liver outcomes. We calculated seven previously developed FI cluster-specific PS, including non-diabetogenic (Preserved Insulin Secretion, Elevated Insulin Secretion, Proinsulin) and diabetogenic clusters (Adiposity-driven Hyperinsulinemia, Visceral Adiposity, Lipodystrophy, Liver/Lipid) in 12,631 participants of the Hispanic Community Healthy Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL), and tested their association with type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular, kidney and liver outcomes. We also tested the association of FI clusters with indices of insulin homeostasis in additional 1,316 Hispanic individuals. Among HCHS/SOL participants (mean age 46 years, 59% women, 20% with diabetes), we validated associations of FI cluster-specific PS and the 19 traits used to generate clusters. The Lipodystrophy cluster was associated with type 2 diabetes (p-value =3.5 x 10-5). In addition, the Adiposity-driven Hyperinsulinemia cluster was associated with the hepatic steatosis index (p-value = 2.2 x1017) and the fatty liver index (p-value = 1.7 x1014), while the Liver/Lipid cluster with liver fibrosis (p-value = 1.5 x104) and lower kidney function (p-value = 5.2 x 10-5). The non-diabetogenic Elevated Insulin Secretion cluster-specific PS was associated with the disposition index (p = 0.0015). These results support insulin resistance mechanisms implicated in type 2 diabetes, liver and kidney outcomes.
